newsitem.title: FRANCE: Commercial court lets Air Liberte fly.
newsitem.headline: Commercial court lets Air Liberte fly.

text.p: A French commercial court decided on Tuesday that ailing carrier Air Liberte would not be wound down, leaving the way open for British Airways and Banque Rivaud to buy the company.
The commercial court met today to decide either to liquidate Air Liberte, in administration since September 26, or to let the company continue its activities.
"The court has decided to maintain the activity and not to turn the administration into a liquidation," court president Dominique Leveque told Reuters by telephone.
"To maintain an activity when it is losing money you need somebody who accepts to support the company," he said.
He said that a statement by British Airways, saying the court had "accepted" its offer for Air Liberte, was excessive and an interpretation.
"The statement by British Airways is totally excessive. It is an interpretation. In a legal sense, there is nothing in the way to stop any other bid than theirs," Leveque told Reuters.
"We are very pleased that the tribunal has agreed that our proposal represents the best way forward for Air Liberte," BA's chief executive Robert Ayling said in a statement issued in London.

British Airways said it and Banque Rivaud would give Air Liberte a 630 million franc capital injection. Mark Rochet, chairman of British Airways' French TAT unit, will become chairman and chief executive of Air Liberte.
BA will get a 70 percent stake and Rivaud 30 percent.
The decision by the court not to wind up Air Liberte is crucial for the bid to succeed but the court itself cannot approve any bid made to the administrators.
The BA/Rivaud offer, the only offer on the table at the moment, has to be approved by Air Liberte's creditors. The creditors are expected to meet by mid-December to take a decision on rescue offers.
Brussels-based Virgin Express, an airline run by Richard Branson, has said it planned to make a higher bid than BA/Rivaud but it has still not made such an offer to the administrators.
The BA and Rivaud offer includes the costs of running Air Liberte while still under administration.
Leveque said that any other bidder would have to pay back the cash advances made by BA and Rivaud to the Air Liberte administrators of some 150 million francs.

Air Liberte, founded by Lotfi Belhassine in 1988, lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996 due to an airfare war and insufficient passenger numbers in the run-up to full liberalisation of French airspace by 1997.
The BA/Rivaud plan aims to get the company back to break-even in 1999. The plan will safeguard 1,250 out of 1,400 jobs at Air Liberte.
